result.summary: Pausanias describes the end of the Phocian or Sacred War under Philip and the razing of Phocian towns. He lists towns made famous by Homer, by Xerxes' burning, or obscure, notes the Phocians' punishment, and recounts their later rebuilding and bravery against the Gauls.

scenes.title: Philip ends the Sacred War
scenes.summary: Philip ends the war in the tenth year after the temple's plunder. Phocian towns are razed, except Abæ, and the Phocians lose their Delphic and Council rights to the Macedonians.
scenes.stakes: The Phocians lose their towns and their standing in the Amphictyonic Council as punishment for the sacrilege.

scenes.title: Rebuilding and later redemption
scenes.summary: The Phocian towns are later rebuilt with Athenian and Theban help. The Phocians fight at Chæronea, Lamia and Crannon, and bravely against the Galati at Delphi.
scenes.stakes: The Phocians seek to atone for their guilt and defend the god at Delphi.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias uses Galati and the Celtic army for the Gauls who invaded Greece.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias says the Phocians' bravery against the Gauls atoned for their old guilt.

analysis.text: The passage shows divine and communal punishment for sacrilege, followed by atonement through defending Delphi.
It records the end of the Third Sacred War in 346 BC, which cemented Macedonian power in Greece.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates events by the Athenian Archon and the Olympiad, as Greek writers commonly did.

language_notes.text: "The course" means the foot-race (the stadion) at the Olympic games; the Olympiad is used as a dating system.
"Rased" is an older spelling of "razed": levelled to the ground.
Homer's Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad lists Phocian towns; the quoted lines are omitted here, marked by the footnote.
The Amphictyonic Council was the league of Greek peoples governing Delphi's temple; Phocian votes passed to Macedon, Philip's kingdom.
The Galati (Gauls) invaded Greece and attacked Delphi in 279 BC; the Phocians' earlier temple plunder is the "guilt" meant.

context_notes.text: Xerxes, king of Persia, invaded Greece in 480 BC and burnt many Phocian towns on his march.
Chæronea (338 BC) was Philip's victory over Athens and Thebes; Lamia and Crannon were battles of 323–322 BC against Antipater, the Macedonian regent.

literary_notes.text: Abæ's innocence is set against the other towns' guilt, explaining why it alone escaped destruction and implying divine justice.
Pausanias interjects his own judgment ("I think"), framing the Phocians' bravery as moral redemption for sacrilege.
